items.title: 6.2 Tangent and Normal to a Curve

source_refs.note: Book p. 173: 6.2 definitions of tangent, point of contact and normal with Figure 6.7 (text before 6.2.1)

blocks.text: If a line touches a curve at exactly one point, it is called a tangent to the curve, and the point is called the point of contact. In Figure 6.7, \(\overleftrightarrow{LM}\) is a tangent to the curve at the point \(P\).

blocks.alt: On a pale yellow panel, magenta X- and Y-axes from 0; a cyan curve with the point P on it; the magenta tangent LM (arrows at both ends, labelled Tangent) and the dark-blue normal PQ (arrows at both ends, labelled Normal) cross at P at right angles, marked 90 degrees.
blocks.caption: Figure 6.7: Tangent LM and normal PQ to a curve at the point P (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 6.7)

blocks.text: The line perpendicular to the tangent at its point of contact is called the normal to the curve at that point. For example, in the Figure 6.7, \(\overleftrightarrow{PQ} \perp \overleftrightarrow{LM}\) at the point \(P\); thus, \(\overleftrightarrow{PQ}\) is the normal to the curve at \(P\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Think of a ruler laid against a round plate: it rests on the edge at one point only. That ruler is a tangent, and the point where it rests is the point of contact.
"Touches at exactly one point" is the right picture for a circle and the other conics. For a general curve, what really matters is that near \(P\) the tangent has the same direction as the curve: its slope is the slope of the curve at \(P\).
The normal is simply the line through the same point \(P\) that makes a right angle with the tangent.
Slopes of the tangent and the normal

Our addition (the book uses these ideas in 6.2.1 to 6.2.3). The slope of the curve at a point is the value of \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) at that point, so
\[m_{T} = \left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)_{(x_{1},\, y_{1})}\]
Two non-vertical perpendicular lines have slopes whose product is \(-1\). So, when \(m_{T} \ne 0\),
\[m_{N} = -\dfrac{1}{m_{T}}\]
Then the point-slope form gives the two lines through \(P(x_{1}, y_{1})\):
\[\text{Tangent: } y - y_{1} = m_{T}(x - x_{1})\]
\[\text{Normal: } y - y_{1} = m_{N}(x - x_{1})\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Two special cases:
If \(m_{T} = 0\), the tangent is horizontal, \(y = y_{1}\), and the normal is vertical, \(x = x_{1}\).
If the tangent is vertical, \(x = x_{1}\), the normal is horizontal, \(y = y_{1}\).
For a circle there is a short cut you will meet again and again: the tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact, so the normal at any point of a circle passes through the centre.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Our illustration (not from the book): the curve \(y = x^{2}\) at the point \((1, 1)\).
\[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 2x, \quad m_{T} = 2(1) = 2\]
Tangent: \(y - 1 = 2(x - 1)\), that is \(2x - y - 1 = 0\).
\[m_{N} = -\dfrac{1}{2}\]
Normal: \(y - 1 = -\frac{1}{2}(x - 1)\), that is \(x + 2y - 3 = 0\).
Check: both lines pass through \((1, 1)\), and \(2 \times \left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) = -1\), so they are perpendicular.

blocks.text:

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Tangent: a line touching the curve at the point of contact \(P\); its slope is \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) at \(P\).
2. Normal: the line through \(P\) perpendicular to the tangent; \(m_{N} = -\frac{1}{m_{T}}\) when \(m_{T} \ne 0\).
3. Both lines pass through the same point \(P\); use the point-slope form.
4. For a circle, the normal at any point passes through the centre.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Taking the normal's slope as \(\frac{1}{m_{T}}\) or \(-m_{T}\). It is the negative reciprocal, \(-\frac{1}{m_{T}}\).
2. Using the general \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) as the slope without putting in the coordinates of \(P\).
3. Forgetting the horizontal and vertical cases: when \(m_{T} = 0\) the normal is \(x = x_{1}\); the formula \(-\frac{1}{m_{T}}\) cannot be used.
